passage: Parveen, don't give me that look. I want this, okay? Chartered accountancy is solid. Abbu built the whole shop keeping his own books; he says his son Imran will be the first real CA in the family. It's the right thing. Yes, I sit on the bike for ten minutes outside the coaching centre every morning before going in. Yes, my stomach does that thing. That's just nerves, everyone has nerves. And the photography? That's a hobby. I sold two prints at the college fest, so what, that's not a career. Last Sunday I spent the whole day shooting the old ghats and didn't look at my phone once, but that's because it was a holiday. Why are you smiling? I'm telling you, I'm happy. I'm fine. I'm fine.

qa.q: What does Imran do every morning outside the coaching centre?
qa.a: He sits on the bike for ten minutes before going in.

qa.q: Why might Imran keep insisting he is happy and fine?
qa.a: Admitting he loves photography more would mean disappointing Abbu, so it feels safer to call the dread 'just nerves' and keep the peace.

qa.q: What could Imran do with those ten minutes on the bike each morning?
qa.a: He could use them to notice honestly what he feels, jot it down for a week, and then talk it through with Parveen or a college counsellor before deciding anything.

qa.q: Why might Parveen be smiling while Imran talks?
qa.a: Parveen probably sees what Imran won't say: the camera days are the ones he lights up on, and 'I'm fine' said twice sounds like the opposite.

grounding: A young man insists he wants the career his father chose while his morning dread and love of photography say otherwise.

passage: I'm Jyoti, and I've shared a hostel room with Ankita for two years. Every morning her alarm goes off at six for the law lectures her parents picked, and every morning she lies there staring at the ceiling fan until 6:20. When her mother calls, she says, "I love it, Mummy, really, it's my dream too." Then she hangs up and goes quiet. On weekends, though, she's a different person. She spends hours at the animal shelter near the college and comes back with muddy jeans, talking nonstop about a three-legged dog. Once I asked if she'd ever thought about veterinary work. She laughed too quickly. "No, no. Law is what I want." I can't see inside her head. But I notice she never talks about law on Sundays.

qa.q: What does Ankita say when her mother calls?
qa.a: "I love it, Mummy, really, it's my dream too."

qa.q: What might Ankita's too-quick laugh suggest?
qa.a: It may suggest the vet idea touched a wish Ankita keeps pushed down, because admitting it could upset her parents and the calm at home.

qa.q: What choice could Ankita make that doesn't mean deciding everything at once?
qa.a: She could quietly note how she feels on lecture mornings versus shelter days, and talk it over with someone she trusts before the next call home.

qa.q: How does Jyoti see Ankita differently from how Ankita describes herself?
qa.a: Jyoti sees two Ankitas, one staring at the fan at six and one talking nonstop about a three-legged dog, while Ankita insists law is what she wants.

grounding: A roommate notices a girl who says law is her dream but dreads each morning and comes alive at the animal shelter.

passage:
June: Irawati's father handed her the admission letter for mechanical engineering, beaming. "Our family's first engineer." She hugged him and wrote in her notebook that night: This is what I want. Good job, me.
September: Every morning at the hostel she woke with a tight chest before workshop class. She told Asif it was the mess food. In the margins of her thermodynamics notes she was sketching costumes, dozens of them, sleeves and collars and pleats.
December: Asif flipped through the notebook and stopped at the sketches. "These are really good. Is this what you actually want?" Irawati opened her mouth to say no. Instead she said, "I don't know. Maybe." It was the first time she had let herself say it aloud.

qa.q: What was Irawati sketching in the margins of her thermodynamics notes?
qa.a: She was sketching costumes, dozens of them, sleeves and collars and pleats.

qa.q: Why did Irawati tell Asif her tight chest came from the mess food?
qa.a: Blaming the food kept her from facing her dread of engineering, the choice that had made her father beam.

qa.q: What was the turning point in December, and what could Irawati do next?
qa.a: When Asif asked what she actually wanted, she admitted 'Maybe'; next she could explore design gently, perhaps through an elective or a counsellor, before speaking to her father.

qa.q: What would change for Irawati's father if she kept saying only 'This is what I want'?
qa.a: He would keep believing his daughter is happy, and might learn the truth much later, when it is harder for both of them.

grounding: Over months, a student writes that she wants the family-approved engineering path while her body and sketches show another wish.

passage:
Harsha, you keep saying you love your engineering course, and you say it a little too often. Let me tell you something.
At twenty I was preparing for the bank exams in Indore. Papa had told the whole mohalla that Gargi would be an officer. And every morning, walking to the coaching centre, I'd say to myself: I want this, I want this. Secure job, respect, peace at home.
But my stomach would knot at the gate. And at night I'd sit at Amma's old sewing machine, cutting patterns out of newspaper, and feel like I could breathe.
I told myself the sewing was just a hobby. Wanting it would upset everyone, so I simply decided I didn't.
It took me six years to admit it. Don't take six years, beta. Just notice which door makes your stomach knot.

qa.q: What did young Gargi do at night at Amma's old sewing machine?
qa.a: Gargi cut patterns out of newspaper and felt able to breathe.

qa.q: Why did young Gargi keep repeating 'I want this' on the way to coaching?
qa.a: Admitting the real wish would upset Papa and everyone at home, so Gargi kept telling the approved story to keep the peace, while the knotted stomach said otherwise.

qa.q: What does Gargi hope Harsha will do differently, and why?
qa.a: Notice early which path brings the knot of dread, instead of taking six years; paying attention to that feeling is the first step to knowing what Harsha actually wants.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt if young Gargi had spoken up about sewing at twenty?
qa.a: Papa might have been disappointed at first, having told the whole mohalla about an officer, but might also have preferred a child who could breathe to one quietly dreading every morning.

grounding: An elder recalls telling themselves they wanted the family-approved bank job while dreading each morning, editing out the wish to sew to keep the peace.

passage:
The hostel's water was off again, the bus to campus left at 7:40, and Raghav had a programming test at nine. He stood in the cold corridor with his toothbrush, heart pounding, the way it did every weekday morning.
'You okay?' Hemant asked, bucket in hand.
'Fine. Just the water.' Raghav smiled. 'Honestly, I'm lucky. Papa's friend's son got a job straight out of this branch. It's a great field. It's what I want.'
Hemant raised an eyebrow. Last night he had seen Raghav at 1 a.m. watching a video on tempering a proper sambar, taking notes.
On the bus, Raghav stared out of the window, reciting sorting algorithms. When the college gate came into view, his chest went tight again. He told himself it was only the test.

qa.q: What was Raghav watching at 1 a.m.?
qa.a: A video on tempering a proper sambar, and he was taking notes.

qa.q: Why might 'It's what I want' feel true to Raghav from the inside?
qa.a: Believing it keeps things smooth with Papa and makes the pounding heart easy to explain away; Raghav files the dread under 'the water' and 'only the test' instead of looking at it.

qa.q: What choice could Raghav make the next time his chest goes tight at the gate?
qa.a: Instead of calling it only the test, he could stop and ask what the dread is really about, perhaps talking honestly with Hemant about the late-night cooking videos.

qa.q: How does Hemant see Raghav's cheerful 'I'm lucky'?
qa.a: Hemant seems doubtful; having seen the 1 a.m. cooking notes, he raises an eyebrow, sensing that Raghav's words don't match what Raghav actually loves.

grounding: A student insists the family-approved branch is what he wants while dreading every morning and hiding his real interest in cooking.

passage: At 5 a.m. the fog over Kanpur was so thick that the street lights looked like smudges, and the power was out again. Abhinav sat on the edge of his bed, CA coaching books stacked by the door, and felt the same heavy stone in his stomach he felt every morning. 'I want this,' he said to the dark room, the way he did most days. 'It's a good, stable career. Papa's right.' He put on his sweater by torchlight. On the way out he passed his old keyboard under its dust cover. His fingers brushed it without his deciding to. His sister Gopika, up early for her own exam, watched from the kitchen door. 'You say you want it,' she said quietly, 'but you look like you're going to the dentist every single day.' 'I'm just tired,' Abhinav said. 'It's the fog.' He shut the door before she could answer.

qa.q: What did Abhinav pass on the way out?
qa.a: He passed his old keyboard under its dust cover.

qa.q: Why does Abhinav keep telling himself 'I want this'?
qa.a: He feels dread every morning, but admitting he doesn't want the career would threaten the peace with Papa, so repeating the line keeps the inconvenient wish buried.

qa.q: What could Abhinav do to hear his own wishes more honestly?
qa.a: He could treat the daily dread as information, talk it through with Gopika or a career counsellor, and then speak with Papa about what he actually wants.

qa.q: How does Gopika see her brother's mornings?
qa.a: Gopika sees that he looks miserable every day, like someone going to the dentist, and she worries his words don't match how he feels.

grounding: A student insists he wants the family-approved career while feeling dread each morning, editing away the wish that would disturb the peace.

passage: Every morning on the metro to her father's wholesale cloth office in Chandni Chowk, Noor told herself the same thing: this is what I want. A secure future, the family business, Abbu proud. She had even told her friend Saurabh that she was lucky. But every morning, somewhere around Kashmere Gate, her chest tightened and her hands went cold. On Sundays she tutored the watchman's two daughters in English, and those were the only hours that flew. When Saurabh asked why she smiled so much talking about the girls' spelling test, she laughed it off. 'It's just a hobby. Real careers are business.' That night she lay awake listing reasons the office was the right choice, and each reason sounded like Abbu's voice, not hers.

qa.q: Where is Noor's father's office?
qa.a: It is a wholesale cloth office in Chandni Chowk.

qa.q: Why does Noor call the tutoring 'just a hobby'?
qa.a: Noor feels drawn to teaching but fears disappointing Abbu, so shrinking the wish to a hobby keeps the peace and hides the dread she feels on the metro.

qa.q: What could Noor do with the signals she's getting?
qa.a: She could treat the cold hands and the joy of Sunday tutoring as real information, and talk honestly with Saurabh or a counsellor before deciding how to speak to Abbu.

qa.a: Saurabh might sense something doesn't fit, since she lights up talking about tutoring but not about the office.

'You're up at six again,' Jatin said, leaning on the kitchen counter. 'Coaching?'
'Yep.' Raghav poured tea without looking at him.
'You don't sound thrilled.'
'I am. It's what I want. Good branch, good job. Everyone says so.'
'Everyone. What do you say?'
'Same thing.' Raghav stirred his tea for too long. 'Why are you asking?'
'Because last night you were up till two watching videos about film editing. And you only sound like this' — Jatin made his voice flat — 'about coaching.'
'Editing's a hobby.'
'You edited Didi's whole wedding film. People cried.'
'Jatin, stop. Papa's already paid the coaching fees. It's decided.'
'You didn't say you wanted it. You said it's decided.'
Raghav put the cup down harder than he meant to. 'I'm going to be late,' he said, and left without finishing his tea.

qa.q: What was Raghav watching until two?
qa.a: He was watching videos about film editing.

qa.q: Why does Raghav stir his tea for too long?
qa.a: He feels uneasy and cornered, because Jatin's questions come close to the wish he has pushed away to keep the family decision calm.

qa.q: What could Raghav do instead of leaving?
qa.a: He could admit what he enjoys, like editing, and ask to talk with Papa about options before the coaching year goes further.

qa.q: How does Jatin see his brother?
qa.a: Jatin sees that Raghav's words and actions don't match, and he cares enough to keep asking.

grounding: A student insists the family-approved engineering path is what he wants, while his brother points to the dread and the editing he loves.

passage:
For most of my first year of CA articleship, I told everyone I loved it. I told myself that most of all.
My parents had framed my foundation result. My father introduced me at weddings as “our future CA, Aadhya.” So when my stomach knotted every morning at the office door, I called it acidity. When I spent lunch breaks sketching sets for the college drama club, I called it a hobby.
My friend Vasudha asked me once, at a chai stall, “When did you last sound happy about balance sheets?” I laughed and changed the subject.
It took a whole year before I let myself finish the sentence I had been editing out: I don't want this. I want to design for theatre.
I haven't told my parents yet. But I've stopped calling the dread acidity.

qa.q: What did Aadhya call the knotted stomach every morning?
qa.a: Aadhya called it acidity.

qa.q: Why did Aadhya keep calling the sketching “a hobby”?
qa.a: Aadhya felt afraid of disappointing proud parents, so it felt calmer to edit out the real wish than to face it.

qa.q: What small step could help Aadhya now?
qa.a: Aadhya could talk with Vasudha or a college counsellor about the theatre interest, and then plan how to share it honestly with the family.

qa.q: How might Vasudha see Aadhya during that first year?
qa.a: Vasudha seemed to notice that Aadhya never sounded happy about the work, and may have felt concerned watching the friend pretend.

grounding: The reflection shows a student insisting on a family-approved career while feeling dread each morning and editing out the real wish.

passage:
Mentor's note, second-year B.Tech, 9 October.
Divyansh has missed four of the last six morning labs. When I asked, he said, “Sir, I really want to be a mechanical engineer. It's my father's dream and mine also. I'm just tired.”
He said “mine also” quickly, twice.
Maria, from his project group, mentioned that he stays until midnight in the music room most days, and is the first to offer to arrange songs for college events. She said he looks “like a different person” there.
In our meeting his shoulders stayed hunched until I asked about music. Then he talked for ten minutes without stopping, smiling.
Next steps: I did not tell him what he wants. I asked him to write down, without editing, what he looks forward to in a week and what he dreads. I have also referred him to the student counselling centre and will meet him again on Friday.

qa.q: How many of the last six morning labs has Divyansh missed?
qa.a: He has missed four of the last six morning labs.

qa.q: Why might Divyansh say “mine also” quickly, twice?
qa.a: He seems anxious to convince himself and others that he wants his father's dream, because admitting otherwise would disturb the peace at home.

qa.q: How could the mentor's writing task help Divyansh?
qa.a: Writing without editing what he looks forward to and dreads could let his real wishes show up before he talks himself out of them.

qa.q: How does Maria see Divyansh?
qa.a: Maria sees a lively, generous musician who seems like a different person in the music room than in labs.

grounding: The mentor's note shows a student insisting he wants the family-approved career while his dread and his real interest show in his behaviour.

Sunday, 11 p.m.
Coaching again tomorrow at 6. I DO want to be a doctor. I've wanted it since Class 8. Ma tells everyone. Bapu has already spoken to the bank about the fees.
So why did I feel sick again when the alarm went this morning? It's just tiredness. Everyone at coaching is tired.
Preeti came into my room today and saw my notebook open to the back page, where I'd drawn another bridge design. She said, “Bhaiya, you never draw hearts and lungs. Only bridges.” I told her to go away.
But she's right, and I hate that she's right. When I think of hospitals I feel heavy. When I think of the new flyover near the station, I want to know how it stands up.
I'm writing this and crossing it out. I'll pretend I didn't write it.
No. I'll leave it.
— Santosh

qa.a: She saw another bridge design drawn on the back page.

qa.q: Why does Santosh keep calling the sick feeling “just tiredness”?
qa.a: He feels scared and guilty about letting down Ma and Bapu, so it is calmer to explain away the dread than to question the plan.

qa.q: What could Santosh do next with what he has written?
qa.a: He could keep the page, talk with Preeti or a school counsellor about his interest in bridges, and then share it with his parents honestly.

qa.q: What might Preeti feel after being told to go away?
qa.a: Preeti might feel hurt but also sure she noticed something true, since she only said what she saw.

grounding: The diary shows a student insisting he wants the family-approved medical career while morning dread and his drawings suggest otherwise.

passage: In Niphad town, everyone knew Vaibhav would take over his father's pharmacy. "It's what I want," he told anyone who asked. Every morning he walked the four streets from home to the shop, and every morning his steps got slower. His stomach felt tight as he raised the shutter. But in the back room, behind the medicine shelves, he kept a tin of wires and old radio parts. When a customer brought in a broken transistor, Vaibhav fixed it in twenty minutes and felt, for the first time that week, completely awake. Nazia, who ran the phone repair stall next door, watched him. "You light up with those wires. You never light up with the pills." "The pharmacy is my future," he said. "Is that you talking, or your father?" Vaibhav didn't answer. He put the radio parts back in the tin and closed the lid, very carefully.

qa.q: How long did it take Vaibhav to fix the transistor?
qa.a: Vaibhav fixed it in twenty minutes.

qa.q: What does Vaibhav's slowing walk and tight stomach suggest he really feels about the pharmacy?
qa.a: They suggest dread, even though he tells everyone the pharmacy is what he wants, because admitting otherwise would upset the family plan.

qa.q: What could Vaibhav try so he stops editing his own wishes?
qa.a: He could admit to himself how alive he feels with electronics, then talk honestly with his father about a way to include it.

qa.q: How might Nazia see the gap between what Vaibhav says and does?
qa.a: Nazia sees clearly that he lights up with the wires, not the pills, and wonders whose wish he is really following.

grounding: A small-town young man insists he wants the family pharmacy while dreading each morning, editing out his real love for electronics.

passage: Paulo was in his second year of law at the university in Lisbon, the career his mother and grandfather had both chosen for him. "Law is my path," he told everyone. But every weekday he woke at six with a heaviness in his chest and lay staring at the ceiling. His flatmate Liam noticed that the only time Paulo whistled was on Sunday, cooking for the whole flat, trying new sauces, tasting, laughing. One Sunday, Liam asked, "Do you ever think about cooking? Like, properly?" Paulo laughed too loudly. "Cooking is a hobby. Law is my future." "You don't whistle on weekdays." Paulo stirred the pan. "I'm just tired on weekdays." "Are you tired, or are you sad?" Paulo put the spoon down. For a moment he looked at the steam rising from the pot. "My mother would never forgive me." "You didn't say you didn't want it," Liam said gently.

qa.q: When was the only time Paulo whistled?
qa.a: Only on Sunday, cooking for the whole flat.

qa.q: Why does Paulo say he is just tired on weekdays?
qa.a: Paulo feels dread and sadness about law, but calling it tiredness hides a wish that would upset his mother.

qa.q: What would you advise Paulo after this conversation?
qa.a: To be honest with himself first about what he wants, maybe by trying a short cooking course, before deciding how to talk to his mother.

qa.q: What might Liam be feeling as he asks these questions?
qa.a: Liam seems caring and a little worried, wanting his friend to stop hiding from himself.

grounding: A student abroad insists law is his path while feeling heavy each morning and alive only when cooking, editing out his real wish to keep peace.

passage:
Every morning that December, the CA coaching centre in Ludhiana smelled of heater dust and chai, and every morning Deepak's stomach turned over on the stairs. He told himself it was the cold.
"You okay?" Gurpreet asked on Tuesday, when Deepak stood by the notice board without going in.
"Totally. This is what I want. Papa's firm, the family name, a stable life. Who wouldn't want that?" He said it quickly, the way he said it at every family wedding.
In the lecture, while the teacher went through tax slabs, Deepak drew the hall's ceiling beams in the margin, then a staircase, then a whole building with a courtyard. When the bell rang he tore the page out and binned it before anyone could see.
"It's just nerves," he told Gurpreet on the way out. "Everyone's stomach hurts before audit."

qa.q: What did Deepak draw in the margin during the lecture?
qa.a: The hall's ceiling beams, then a staircase, then a whole building with a courtyard.

qa.q: Why might Deepak insist "This is what I want"?
qa.a: Deepak feels dread each morning, but calling the family plan his own wish keeps the peace and spares him the guilt and fear of disappointing Papa; binning the drawing hides the other wish even from himself.

qa.q: What could help Deepak hear his own wishes?
qa.a: He could notice the pattern honestly, the dread on the stairs and the buildings in the margins, write down what he actually enjoys, and talk it through with a counsellor or someone he trusts.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet read Deepak's quick "Totally"?
qa.a: Gurpreet saw Deepak frozen by the notice board and heard a very fast answer, so Gurpreet may sense something is off without knowing what.

grounding: A student insists he wants the family-approved career while feeling dread every morning and hiding a different wish.
